summary: This proposed standard describes two methods for encapsulating network interconnect traffic, such as IP, over ATM Adaptation Layer 5. It was replaced by RFC 2684.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how to carry IP packets and bridged frames over an ATM network. It gives two choices: put a small header in front of every packet so several protocols can share one ATM connection, or give each protocol its own connection and add nothing to the packet at all.

questions: what is llc encapsulation over atm
how is ip carried over atm aal5
subtitle: How routed and bridged packets are carried over an ATM network, either one protocol per circuit or many on one circuit.

tldr.problem: ATM networks carry fixed-size cells, so a variable-length IP or bridged frame has to be put into something that can be segmented and reassembled, and the receiver has to be able to tell which protocol the payload holds.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two methods. LLC Encapsulation puts an IEEE 802.2 LLC header, and sometimes a SNAP header, in front of each packet so several protocols can share one virtual circuit. VC Based Multiplexing leaves the payload alone and gives each protocol its own virtual circuit.
tldr.outcome: Either method lets an ATM network carry IP and other protocols, and the choice depends on whether creating many virtual circuits is cheap. The document has been replaced by RFC 2684.

today: RFC 1483 was a Proposed Standard published in July 1993. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2684, which is the current specification of multiprotocol encapsulation over ATM AAL5.

sections.title: Two Ways to Carry Traffic over ATM
sections.content:
Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) based networks are of increasing interest for both local and wide area applications. The memo describes two different methods for carrying connectionless network interconnect traffic, routed and bridged Protocol Data Units (PDUs), over an ATM network.

The first method, LLC Encapsulation, allows multiplexing of multiple protocols over a single ATM virtual circuit. The protocol of a carried PDU is identified by prefixing the PDU with an IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) header. A subset of this method was earlier defined for SMDS.

The second method, VC Based Multiplexing, does higher-layer protocol multiplexing implicitly through ATM Virtual Circuits (VCs): each protocol is carried over a separate virtual circuit, so nothing has to be added to the payload.

ATM is a cell based transfer mode that requires variable length user information to be segmented and reassembled to and from short, fixed length cells. This memo does not specify a new Segmentation And Reassembly method for bridged and routed PDUs. Instead the PDUs are carried in the Payload field of the Common Part Convergence Sublayer (CPCS) PDU of ATM Adaptation Layer type 5 (AAL5). The memo only describes how routed and bridged PDUs are carried directly over the CPCS of AAL5, that is, when the Service Specific Convergence Sublayer of AAL5 is empty.
sections.plainLanguage: Two choices are on the table. Either every packet gets a small header saying what protocol it holds, so one ATM connection can carry several protocols, or each protocol gets its own ATM connection and the packet is left exactly as it is.

sections.title: Choosing the Multiplexing Method
sections.content:
The RFC expects VC Based Multiplexing to be dominant in environments where dynamic creation of large numbers of ATM VCs is fast and economical, and says these conditions are likely to first prevail in private ATM networks.

LLC Encapsulation, on the other hand, may be desirable when it is not practical for one reason or another to have a separate VC for each carried protocol. That is the case, for example, if the ATM network only supports semi-permanent or permanent virtual circuits (PVCs), or if charging depends heavily on the number of simultaneous VCs.

When two ATM stations wish to exchange connectionless network interconnect traffic, the selection of the multiplexing method is done either by manual configuration, in the case of PVCs, or by B-ISDN signalling procedures, in the case of switched VCs. The RFC notes that the details of B-ISDN signalling were still under study in CCITT, but that B-ISDN signalling messages can be assumed to include a low layer compatibility information element, which will allow negotiation of AAL5 and the carried encapsulation protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Use one connection per protocol when setting up connections is cheap. Use a header on every packet when it is not, for example when the network only offers permanent connections or charges by connection.

sections.title: The AAL5 Frame Format
sections.content:
No matter which multiplexing method is selected, routed and bridged PDUs are encapsulated within the Payload field of the AAL5 CPCS-PDU. The Payload field contains user information up to 2^16 - 1 octets.

The PAD field pads the CPCS-PDU to fit exactly into the ATM cells, so that the last 48 octet cell payload created by the SAR sublayer has the CPCS-PDU Trailer right justified in the cell. It holds 0 to 47 octets.

The CPCS-UU, or User-to-User indication, field is used to transparently transfer CPCS user to user information. The field has no function under the multiprotocol ATM encapsulation described in the memo and can be set to any value. The CPI, or Common Part Indicator, field aligns the CPCS-PDU trailer to 64 bits, and when only that alignment function is used the field shall be coded as 0x00.

The Length field indicates the length in octets of the Payload field. The maximum value for the Length field is 65535 octets, and a Length field coded as 0x00 is used for the abort function. The CRC field protects the entire CPCS-PDU except the CRC field itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Whatever is carried, it goes in the payload of an AAL5 frame. The frame ends with a small trailer that says how long the payload was and checks it for damage.

sections.title: LLC Encapsulation
sections.content:
LLC Encapsulation is needed when several protocols are carried over the same VC. So that the receiver can process the incoming CPCS-PDU, the Payload field must identify the protocol of the routed or bridged PDU, and in LLC Encapsulation that information is encoded in an LLC header placed in front of the carried PDU.

For routed protocols the PDU is identified by prefixing it with an IEEE 802.2 LLC header, which may be followed by an IEEE 802.1a SubNetwork Attachment Point (SNAP) header. In LLC Type 1 operation the LLC header consists of three one octet fields, DSAP, SSAP and Ctrl, and the Control field always has the value 0x03, specifying an Unnumbered Information Command PDU.

The LLC header value 0xFE-FE-03 identifies that a routed ISO PDU follows. The routed ISO protocol is then identified by a one octet NLPID field that is part of the Protocol Data, with NLPID values administered by ISO and CCITT and defined in ISO/IEC TR 9577. An NLPID value of 0x00 is defined as the Null Network Layer or Inactive Set, and since it has no significance in this encapsulation scheme it is invalid under the ATM encapsulation.

IP is not carried that way, even though it has an NLPID value of 0xCC: the RFC says that format must not be used, and IP is encapsulated like all other routed non-ISO protocols by identifying it in the SNAP header that immediately follows the LLC header. The presence of a SNAP header is indicated by the LLC header value 0xAA-AA-03. A SNAP header holds a three-octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) and a two octet Protocol Identifier (PID), which together identify a distinct routed or bridged protocol. The OUI value 0x00-00-00 specifies that the following PID is an EtherType, and for an Internet IP PDU the EtherType value is 0x08-00. The memo notes that this is compatible with RFC 1042.

For bridged protocols the type of the bridged media is identified in the SNAP header instead. The OUI value is the 802.1 organization code 0x00-80-C2 and the actual media type is specified by the two octet PID, which also indicates whether the original Frame Check Sequence is preserved within the bridged PDU. Padding is added after the PID field if necessary, to align the user information field of the bridged PDU at a four octet boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet on a shared connection starts with three bytes that name the protocol, and usually four more bytes that narrow it down. For IP those bytes are the LLC value 0xAA-AA-03 and the EtherType 0x08-00.

sections.title: VC Based Multiplexing
sections.content:
In VC Based Multiplexing the carried network interconnect protocol is identified implicitly by the VC connecting the two ATM stations: each protocol must be carried over a separate VC. There is therefore no need to include explicit multiplexing information in the Payload of the AAL5 CPCS-PDU, which results in minimal bandwidth and processing overhead. The carried protocol can be manually configured or negotiated dynamically during call establishment using signalling procedures.

PDUs of routed protocols are carried as they are in the Payload of the AAL5 CPCS-PDU. PDUs of bridged protocols are carried exactly as in the LLC Encapsulation case, except that only the fields after the PID field are included. Because the PID field is not included, the presence or absence of the trailing LAN FCS must be identified implicitly by the VC: PDUs with the LAN FCS and PDUs without it are considered to belong to different protocols even if the bridged media type would be the same.

The RFC also covers bridging in an ATM network. An ATM interface acting as a bridge must be able to flood, forward and filter bridged PDUs. Flooding is performed by sending the PDU to all possible appropriate destinations, which in the ATM environment means sending it through each relevant VC, either by explicitly copying it to each VC or by using a multicast VC. To forward a PDU, a bridge must be able to associate a destination MAC address with a VC. Because it is unreasonable, and perhaps impossible, to require bridges to statically configure an association of every possible destination MAC address with a VC, ATM bridges must provide enough information for an ATM interface to learn dynamically about foreign destinations. To do that, a bridged PDU shall conform to the LLC encapsulation, so that the receiving ATM interface knows to look into the bridged PDU and learn the association between the foreign destination and an ATM station.
sections.plainLanguage: With one connection per protocol, the packet is copied into the frame with nothing added. The connection itself says what protocol it carries, so there is nothing to strip off at the other end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is brief on this point: security issues are not addressed in this memo. The document says only that the details related to the negotiation of the multiplexing method as well as address resolution had to be left for further RFCs, because of incomplete standardization of ATM multicasting, addressing and signalling mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about security. It leaves the details of negotiating the method and of resolving addresses to later documents.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF THE AAL5 CPCS-PDU

items.title: Payload
items.text: The user information: up to 2^16 - 1 octets.

items.title: PAD
items.text: 0 to 47 octets, padding the CPCS-PDU to fit exactly into the ATM cells.

items.title: CPCS-UU
items.text: 1 octet of user-to-user indication, with no function here.

items.title: CPI
items.text: 1 octet aligning the CPCS-PDU trailer to 64 bits; coded as 0x00 when only alignment is used.

items.title: Length
items.text: 2 octets giving the length of the Payload field; 0x00 is used for the abort function.

items.title: CRC
items.text: 4 octets protecting the whole CPCS-PDU except the CRC field itself.
